title: The Example
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 27 of 40
content:
Maxson looked at Danse and saw an enemy.

Danse looked at Maxson and saw home.

That was why the confrontation hurt to watch.

The elder entered Listening Post Bravo alone, though I had no doubt soldiers waited above. His coat was damp from the rain. His hand rested near his weapon.

Danse immediately came to attention.

Reflex.

Years of training stronger than humiliation.

“Elder.”

Maxson’s face hardened.

“Don’t call me that.”

Danse flinched.

I stepped closer to him.

Maxson noticed.

“So this is how it is.”

“This is how what is?” I asked.

“You were ordered to execute a synth infiltrator.”

“I found Danse.”

“You found a machine wearing his face.”

Danse went rigid.

I felt anger rise.

Before I could speak, Danse did.

“He’s right.”

I turned on him.

“No.”

“Stay out of this.”

“Absolutely not.”

Maxson’s gaze moved between us.

“Paladin Danse is dead. He was never real.”

Something in Danse’s face collapsed.

I stepped forward.

“He was real enough to command your recon team.”

“Because the Institute designed him to deceive.”

“Then they did a terrible job, because he has spent years trying to destroy them.”

“You don’t know his purpose.”

“Neither do you.”

Maxson’s eyes sharpened.

“I know what he is.”

Danse’s voice came low.

“Elder, after everything I’ve done—”

Maxson rounded on him.

“You expect your service to excuse your nature?”

“No.”

The answer was immediate.

Danse straightened.

“If my death protects the Brotherhood, I accept it.”

I felt physically sick.

Maxson looked almost relieved.

Of course Danse would obey.

That was the tragedy.

“I don’t,” I said.

Both men looked at me.

Danse’s expression became furious.

“This isn’t your decision.”

“Yes, it is. You told me to do it.”

“You have your orders.”

“And I refuse them.”

Maxson stepped closer.

“Then you place yourself against the Brotherhood.”

“No. I place one person above one bad order.”

“That is how organizations rot.”

“Then maybe organizations should survive questions.”

Danse whispered my name designation in warning.

I ignored him.

“Look at him,” I told Maxson.

“I am.”

“No. You’re looking at a category. Look at him.”

Maxson’s jaw tightened.

“Danse would have killed a synth under these circumstances.”

The statement hit all three of us.

Because it was true.

Danse closed his eyes.

I swallowed.

“Yes,” I said. “And maybe finding out what that feels like is part of why he deserves the chance to become better.”

Danse looked at me.

Pain, anger, understanding.

Maxson said nothing.

I continued.

“If the Institute wanted an infiltrator, why give him a life that made him loyal to you? Why let him bleed beside your soldiers? Why let him lose people and grieve them? Why build someone capable of choosing death for your ideals?”

“Programming.”

“Then humans are just training and chemistry with better marketing.”

Maxson’s hand moved toward his weapon.

Danse stepped between us.

“Enough.”

He faced Maxson.

“I won’t allow bloodshed over me.”

“You don’t get to order me anymore,” I said.

Danse’s mouth tightened.

“Habit.”

Even then.

Even there.

The stupid callback nearly broke me.

Maxson stared at Danse for a long time.

Then his hand moved away from the weapon.

“You cannot return.”

Danse did not move.

“You are stripped of rank, authority, and Brotherhood protection. If you approach our installations, you will be treated as hostile.”

Each sentence removed a piece of him.

Danse stood through all of them.

“Yes, sir.”

Maxson’s expression flickered.

Maybe regret.

Maybe anger.

Maybe nothing I had the right to name.

He looked at me.

“You are responsible for him.”

I almost laughed at the irony.

“I have been for a while.”

Danse shot me a look.

Maxson turned and left.

The elevator doors closed above us.

Silence filled the bunker.

Danse remained at attention.

“Danse.”

Nothing.

I touched his shoulder.

His knees gave out.

I caught him badly.

We ended up on the floor together, Danse half against me, one hand gripping my sleeve.

He did not cry this time.

That would have been easier.

He stared at the wall.

“It’s gone.”

“What?”

“Everything.”

“No.”

“My rank. My unit. My home.”

“Not everything.”

He looked at me.

I knew what he wanted me to say.

Me.

Us.

Love.

I refused to turn myself into a consolation prize.

“You still have yourself,” I said.

Danse laughed once, without humor.

“That’s the part I’m least certain exists.”

I held his face between my hands.

“Then we find out.”

He closed his eyes.

“What if I don’t like the answer?”

“Then you keep looking.”

His hands covered mine.

For the first time since I met him, Paladin Danse had no mission.

Only a life.

It frightened him more.

Maxson’s departure left a sound behind.

Not literal footsteps.

Authority.

For hours afterward Danse kept turning toward the elevator as if another order might descend and tell him what came next.

None did.

I heated water because making tea felt less offensive than making his coffee.

He sat at the table with his holotags in front of him.

The Brotherhood emblem caught the bunker light.

“Do you want those?” I asked.

His fingers closed around the metal.

“Yes.”

I had expected hesitation.

“Even now?”

“Especially now.”

He looked at the tag.

“This was mine.”

The statement was simple and fierce.

“Whatever else is false, I wore this. I earned the rank attached to it. The missions happened.”

“Good.”

His gaze sharpened.

“Good?”

“You sounded like you for a second.”

He looked down again.

“I don’t know what that means anymore.”

“Neither do I. Keep going.”

Danse turned the tag over between thumb and forefinger.

“I remember my first day at the Citadel.”

“Okay.”

“I remember being terrified I would fail inspection.”

“Very on-brand.”

A faint exhale.

“I remember Cutler hiding one of my boots.”

I smiled.

“I remember earning my first promotion. I remember the pride.”

His voice shook.

“If those memories belonged to someone else first, does that make the pride theft?”

“No.”

“You answered quickly.”

“Because whoever supplied the memory didn’t stand through your inspection. You did.”

Danse looked at me.

“The memory may have put you in the room. The choice to keep showing up afterward was yours.”

He frowned.

“You keep separating origin from action.”

“Yes.”

“Convenient.”

“For you? Extremely.”

That earned the ghost of a smile.

We drank the tea.

It was terrible in a different way than his coffee.

Neither of us complained.

Later, while I checked the bunker’s upper entrance, Danse followed me with his rifle.

“You don’t have to patrol,” I said.

“We need security.”

“We also need you to sleep.”

“I won’t.”

“Then lie down and fail at it horizontally.”

He gave me a look.

I kept inspecting the door.

At the top of the stairs, cold night air drifted through the ruins. No vertibird lights crossed the sky.

Danse stood beside me without armor, suddenly vulnerable in a way I hated.

“Maxson spared me because of you,” he said.

“Maxson chose not to kill you.”

“Because you forced the issue.”

“Don’t make my argument erase his decision.”

Danse was silent.

I looked at him.

“You told me once command means living with consequences. So does mercy.”

“He may regret it.”

“Maybe.”

“I may prove him wrong.”

“Maybe.”

“You have got to stop saying that.”

“No.”

His mouth twitched.

Wind moved across the broken concrete.

“Do you regret it?” he asked.

“What?”

“Refusing the order.”

I thought about the Prydwen, Haylen, Rhys, the possibility that the Brotherhood would never welcome me again. I thought about the weapon I had carried into the bunker in case Maxson’s fear proved true.

“No.”

Danse searched my face.

“Not even a little?”

“I’m scared. That’s different.”

He nodded slowly.

“I’m scared too.”

That was new.

Not *concerned*. Not *assessing risk.*

Scared.

I leaned against him.

He hesitated, then put an arm around me.

No rank.

No orders.

Two frightened people in a ruined building, trying not to confuse certainty with courage.

We stayed outside longer than either of us needed to.

Danse watched the road Maxson had taken.

“Do you think he meant it?” he asked.

“What?”

“That I should stay out of the Brotherhood’s sight.”

“Yes.”

His jaw tightened.

“And if they see me?”

“I don’t know.”

He nodded as if uncertainty were an order he could obey.

Then he looked down at his empty chest where the Brotherhood insignia would normally have been.

“I spent years believing exile was something that happened to people who failed.”

“You didn’t fail.”

“Maxson would disagree.”

“Maxson is allowed to be wrong.”

That earned me a faint, disbelieving laugh.

“You say that very easily.”

“I’ve had practice.”

Danse looked toward the bunker door.

“I don’t know what I am supposed to be now.”

“Cold, apparently.”

He blinked.

I bumped my shoulder against his.

“One problem at a time.”

The first step toward the bunker made him stop.

“What?” I asked.

“My tags.”

He touched the place where Brotherhood holotags usually rested beneath his uniform.

“They took them?”

“No. I left them inside.”

“Want them?”

He thought.

“Yes.”

Not because Maxson recognized the service anymore. Because Danse did.

That distinction seemed important enough not to say aloud.

After a while Danse said, “We should go inside. Temperature is dropping.”

“Romantic.”

“Hypothermia is not.”

“See? Still you.”

He looked down at me.

This time the smile stayed.
